lead: On a Friday of the Resurrection season the Church still looks at the Cross, now with Easter eyes. Paul says that the message of the Cross looks like foolishness, yet it is the power and wisdom of God. In the Gospel Jesus tells of a sower whose seed seems to be wasted on path, rock and thorns, and yet the harvest is beyond all expectation. Both readings teach the same patience of God: what looks weak and lost is where his power is at work. The words to watch are foolishness, power and listen.

set: Corinth was a rich and busy port city in Greece, where public speakers and teachers of wisdom were admired. The Christians there had begun to divide into groups, each attached to a favourite preacher: “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos” (1:12). Paul answers by going to the centre: the Gospel is not one more school of clever speech. Its heart is a crucified Messiah, and that turns the world’s measure of wisdom upside down.
str: v. 18: the thesis: the word of the Cross is foolishness to some, the power of God to others.
vv. 19–20: Scripture and three questions: where are the wise?
v. 21: God chose to save believers through the “foolishness” of preaching.
vv. 22–24: signs, wisdom, and Christ crucified, the power and wisdom of God.
kw: Literally “the word of the cross”. Paul does not preach a theory about the Cross; he proclaims a person who was crucified.
Related to the word from which “moron” comes. To a cultured ear in Corinth, a crucified saviour sounded absurd: crucifixion was the death of slaves and rebels.

A trap or an obstacle on the road. For many devout Jews of Paul’s day, a Messiah who died under a curse (see Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13) was hard to accept. Paul, himself a Jew, had once stumbled at it.
vv: For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
Note the tenses: “being saved” is a road we are on. Salvation has begun and is still going on in us.
For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”
Paul quotes Isaiah 29:14 largely in its Greek form. God has always overturned human pride.

Not a successful hero, not a clever argument, but “Christ crucified”. The Greek participle suggests one who was crucified and remains the Crucified, even in his risen glory, as the risen Lord still bears his wounds.
but to those who are the called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.
God’s call crosses every line. The first believers were Jews, and Gentiles were added to them.
ch: The Catechism teaches that God showed his almighty power above all in the voluntary humiliation and Resurrection of his Son, and quotes the verse that follows today’s reading: the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men (CCC 272). The Church does not hide the Cross after Easter. In the East Syriac tradition the Cross is honoured as the sign of victory and of the Lord’s glorious return; the risen Lord is the Crucified who conquered.

r.h: A sower went out to sow
set: This is the first long parable in Mark’s Gospel. Jesus teaches from a boat on the Sea of Galilee, with the crowd on the shore. Mark has already shown that some people are opposed to Jesus, others are confused, and some follow him (chapters 2–3). The parable speaks to that situation: why does the word bear fruit in some hearts and not in others? The explanation of the parable comes in vv. 13–20, which are not part of today’s reading.
str: vv. 1–2: the setting: a boat, a crowd, teaching in parables.
vv. 4–7: three losses: the path, the rocky ground, the thorns.
v. 8: the good soil and the great harvest.
v. 9: “Let anyone with ears to hear listen!”
kw: In the background is the Hebrew mashal: a comparison, a riddle, a story that makes the listener think. A parable does not explain everything; it invites.
The parable begins and ends with a call to hear. Every devout Jew prayed daily, “Hear, O Israel” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Hearing in the Bible means receiving and obeying.
An extraordinary harvest. When Isaac reaped a hundredfold, it was a sign of God’s blessing (Genesis 26:12). The point is not farming skill, but the abundance of God’s kingdom.
vv: “Listen! A sower went out to sow.
The sower is generous, even careless by human standards. He scatters seed everywhere. God does not hold back his word from anyone.
And when the sun rose, it was scorched; and since it had no root, it withered away.
Quick enthusiasm without roots does not last. The heat that should help the plant grow destroys it.
Other seed fell into good soil and brought forth grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirty and sixty and a hundredfold.
Three failures, but the story ends in a harvest that more than makes up for every loss. That is the hope of the parable.
ch: The Catechism says that the parables are like mirrors for us: will we be hard soil or good earth? Jesus asks for a decision, and to know the secrets of the kingdom one must become his disciple (CCC 546). The Second Vatican Council compares the word of God to a seed sown in a field: those who hear it with faith and are joined to the little flock of Christ have received the kingdom itself (Lumen Gentium 5, in substance).

qa: Why does the sower waste so much seed?

The parable is not a lesson in efficient farming. It shows God’s generosity: he sows his word in every heart, even where it seems useless. He does not first choose the good soil and ignore the rest. Our task is to become good soil, and to sow as generously as he does.
study: Where in my life does the Cross still look like foolishness to me, and where have I seen it as the power of God?
Which of the four soils best describes how I received God’s word this week? What would help it take root?
